purpose: Rifabutin is an antibiotic used mainly to prevent or treat a serious bacterial infection called Mycobacterium avium complex, or MAC, which often affects people with HIV or weakened immune systems. It can also be used as part of a combination treatment for tuberculosis (TB). Your doctor may prescribe it to keep you from getting sick if your immune system is not working well.
how_it_works: Rifabutin works by getting inside the bacteria and blocking a key enzyme the bacteria need to make copies of themselves. Without this enzyme, the bacteria cannot grow or multiply. Over time, this stops the infection from spreading and helps your body fight it off.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include upset stomach, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and loss of appetite. You may also notice your urine, sweat, tears, or saliva turning orange or reddish-brown — this is harmless but can permanently stain soft contact lenses. Some people also get muscle aches, headache, or a skin rash.
warnings: Tell your doctor right away if you notice eye problems like pain or blurred vision, since rifabutin can rarely cause eye inflammation. It can lower your white blood cell and platelet counts, so watch for signs of infection or unusual bruising or bleeding. This drug interacts with many other medications — including HIV drugs and birth control pills — so always tell your doctor and pharmacist everything you are taking. Do not take it if you are allergic to rifabutin or similar antibiotics like rifampin.
typical_dosing: The usual adult dose for preventing MAC infection is 300 mg taken by mouth once a day, with or without food. If it bothers your stomach, you can take it in two smaller doses of 150 mg twice a day. Your doctor may adjust your dose depending on other medications you take or your specific condition. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions.
